title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (200 pairs) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, the Mininet 10% holdout that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models promises operational productivity but also raises safety risks when generated changes are semantically incorrect or violate workflow constraints. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? We executed a paired design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, issuing one automated repair prompt on the identical candidate. Primary contributions: (1) a sealed, preregistered paired experiment with full execution accounting; (2) an artifact‑grounded clarification of how adapter‑enforced determinism was realized and how that choice affects inference; (3) an evidence‑backed discussion of when and why deterministic GVR is operationally useful.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies across LLM applications document hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism and recommend verifier‑assisted repair and constrained agent patterns to improve safety. NetOps prototypes demonstrate feasibility for intent→configuration translation but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectural proposals advocate integrating generation with deterministic checkers (Batfish‑style) and guarded agent frameworks; independent red‑team audits show configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection risks. Our study situates itself as an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validator+repair on a fixed generator output, addressing a gap between architectural proposals and instrumented failure‑rate evidence in representative NetOps tasks.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The experiment was preregistered as cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02 and fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with bootstrap_seed = 1729.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks; four topology clusters). The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and workflow constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal validator blind spots.

Determinism and adapter semantics (reviewer clarification). Model configuration metadata lists the declared model as gpt‑5‑mini and records a null temperature field; determinism for the paired contrast was enforced by the orchestration adapter rather than by sampling on the model side. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics so that a single initial candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions for each task. This enforcement is recorded in the archived reconciliation and accounting artifacts (see deterministic_reconciliation.json and the adapter/provider audit fields that report hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation: 200). In short: temperature metadata in the model configuration is not the sole determinant of deterministic behavior here—adapter semantics produced the single shared initial invocation per task; archived adapter accounting artifacts demonstrate that enforcement.

Repair policy and contamination handling. If the primary validator reported violations, the preregistered policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM and required re‑validation of any repaired candidate. The Mininet holdout served as an independent contamination detector; the preregistered conservative rule excluded pairs where validator verdict != Mininet verdict from the primary analysis. The contamination summary artifact reports zero disagreement flags for that holdout. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact set does not include the explicit randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout, preventing bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which tasks comprised the 10% sample even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements.

Statistical implementation note for degenerate paired tables. When discordant counts are zero (n10 = n01 = 0) the exact McNemar test yields p = 1.0 and paired bootstrap percentile CIs may be degenerate. We report the exact McNemar result and bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed recorded) as preregistered; these quantities are artifact‑grounded and reflect the observed degenerate contingency.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). Adapter/provider accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming a single shared initial invocation per task. Model calls used = 200 (one shared generation per task); allowed repair calls = up to 200 but repair_calls_used = 0.

Validator outcomes and primary contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Under the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test the p‑value = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. These results are recorded in the analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Contamination check and emulator holdout. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout produced zero validator–emulator disagreements per the contamination summary artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv). As noted, the explicit selection seed used to draw that holdout is not present as a labeled artifact, which limits exact deterministic reconstruction of the held‑out indices despite the zero‑disagreement result.

Repair and secondary estimands. Because no validator failures occurred, the repair branch was never invoked and the preregistered secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data in this run; the analysis bundle records these secondary results as empty.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed null (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded outcome: the generator+prompt policy used here produced validator‑satisfying candidates for every curated task when sampled once deterministically per the adapter contract. This outcome does not imply automated repair is unnecessary in general; rather, it demonstrates that the marginal utility of GVR depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the evaluated workload and generation policy.

Why the degenerate result occurred. Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count matched required_command_count across tasks and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for diverse difficulty labels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard"), indicating the task bank exercised nontrivial dependency constraints while the generator outputs satisfied those constraints. Adapter accounting confirms single shared initial generation, removing sampling variance as a route to produce failing candidates. The Mininet holdout found no disagreements in the drawn sample, consistent with validator coverage for the sampled inputs but limited in generality by holdout size and the missing selection seed.

Methodological tradeoffs and practitioner guidance. The paired shared_initial design isolates the marginal effect of validator+repair on an identical candidate but excludes benefits that could arise from multi‑sample generation, higher sampling temperature, model ensembles, or multiple repair iterations. For operational assurance, we recommend: (1) measure unconditional baseline failure rates using independent per‑condition multi‑draw sampling when the objective is unconditional risk estimation; (2) scale emulator/real‑device corroboration and record selection seeds for reproducibility; (3) expand validator fidelity (vendor semantics, device models) and consider larger repair budgets or human escalation when baseline failures are nontrivial.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired study (n = 200) comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline for intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with adapter‑enforced shared_initial generation. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that deterministic GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent; when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under a chosen generation policy, an automated single‑attempt repair budget yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory runs should target workloads with measurable baseline failures, allow multi‑sample/multi‑step repair designs, expand emulator corroboration, and evaluate multiple models to characterize practical operational gains.

The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
